posts.caption: The trailer was hitched by 8:15 and I'd braided her forelock the night before, which is the kind of optimism I should have outgrown. At 8:55 she was in the far corner of the paddock examining a patch of clover. At 9:10 she was thinking about it at the foot of the ramp. At 9:35 she walked on like it was her idea and looked back at the line of rigs waiting behind me. We pulled in just as the first class was being called. She did not care. She never has.
posts.first: My friend with the show barn once told me a good trailer horse loads in under a minute. I laughed so hard I had to sit on the hitch. Mine has loaded in anywhere from four minutes to an hour and a half. It has never once been because she couldn't.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a glossy chestnut mare with a long wavy blonde mane and a gold earring, standing at the ramp of an open horse trailer and glancing sideways with a smirk. Text at the top reads: The trailer leaves at nine. I load at nine-forty. They call it stalling. I call it an entrance.

posts.caption: The first spring I had him, he'd pull the reins out of my hands the second we cleared the gate, and I'd laugh like a teenager the whole way across the back forty. These days we leave at a walk and I get off twice to check a gate that is already closed. He waits for me each time and acts like it's his idea to stop. Last Sunday a hawk rose out of the tall grass right beside us. He lifted one ear, looked at it, and kept walking. I cried a little. I blame the wind.
posts.first: I had my knee looked at in August and the doctor said no more jumping, and I think I felt relieved before I felt sad. The old gray gelding has not heard this news and still stops at the same fence every ride like he's waiting for me to change my mind.

posts.quote: I keep carrots in the truck for emergencies. The horse has decided that anytime I'm near the truck is an emergency.
posts.first: I drive a nine-year-old truck with a cracked dash and a bag of carrots rolling around under the passenger seat. Last week the feed store clerk asked why the whole cab smells like a salad. I told him I didn't want to get into it. The horse can smell the truck from the creek.

posts.caption: She had every intention of riding today. I know this because she laid out her boots by the back door and checked the radar twice before the coffee finished. The first drop hit the barn roof at 11:20, forty minutes ahead of schedule, and I heard the whole lean of her disappointment from across the yard. She came out in her rain jacket anyway, stood in my aisle, and fed me peppermints until the gutters ran over. We called it a ride. I have never felt more respected.
posts.first: My husband asked once why I keep the weather app on my phone's first page. I told him it's the barn's morning paper. He still checks it after me, just to see if I got it wrong. I haven't, not about rain. I've been wrong about everything else.

posts.caption: The trainer drove forty minutes to teach us leading, which she described on the phone as a quick refresher. By the second lap of the arena I could tell she'd stopped taking notes. Big Red picked the route, the pace, and the corner where she'd pause to look at the cones like she'd paid for them. The trainer kept her face very calm and very kind. At the end she coiled the rope, said we should work on our partnership, and asked for a glass of water. I gave her two.
posts.first: I've been paying for lessons with that trainer since 2017. She told me the first day that every horse eventually decides who is in charge, and the only choice you get is whether it's a good decision. I wrote that on a feed-store receipt and taped it inside the tack room.

posts.caption: The hay net came with a promise on the package: eight hours of slow, steady chewing. I hung it at seven, checked the latch twice, and walked up to the house for the dishes. Pudding watched me go with the face of a pony who had already seen the end of the movie. By the time I'd rinsed the second pot, I could hear the empty net bumping the stall door like a tiny knock. I went back out. He looked at me, then at the net, then at me again. We both pretended we'd run the test fairly.
posts.first: Every pony I've owned has treated the product label as a challenge. I once bought a bucket guaranteed to be tip-proof and found it three stalls away within the hour. I keep the receipts in a drawer. Pudding is the only one who can read them.

Headline: The slow-feeder hay net is supposed to last all night. Subtitle: I finished it before she walked back to the house.
